extracted.intended_audience: intellectual property practitioners, design applicants, and in-house counsel preparing International Design Applications under the Hague System
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and practical criteria for preparing and prosecuting International Design Applications (IDAs) under the Hague System, with emphasis on the required reproductions, disclosure, and cross‑jurisdictional pitfalls. Aimed at ensuring formal compliance at WIPO and anticipating national IPO examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal review of reproductions at WIPO (Rule 9 requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO assesses whether the International Design Application meets the requirements of the Hague Agreement (Rule 9). A design can be displayed with photos or other graphics and each view must be a separate reproduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reproductions must be of sufficient quality and all details must be clearly distinguishable. Rule 9 requires a separate reproduction for each view. Use reproductions that unambiguously show the design from required angles. For contracting parties with different representation requirements, make a specific statement in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure under local examination (insufficient reproductions ground for refusal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Rule 9 generally prevents refusal based on choice of representations, contracting countries may refuse an IDA if the reproductions are deemed insufficient to fully disclose the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a substantial proportion of IDAs face refusal on insufficient disclosure grounds at national IPOs. Plan reproductions to meet strict national disclosure standards when designating jurisdictions known to require full disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries require full disclosure: the set of reproductions must provide full disclosure of the design or the application can be rejected unless the applicant adds required reproductions within a timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a feature is not shown in the reproductions it may not be protected in jurisdictions requiring full disclosure (e.g., USPTO, Japan, South Korea, Russia). In other jurisdictions, parts not shown are simply not protected. Consider including all relevant sides (e.g., bottom/back) at filing if design law in target jurisdictions requires full disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of views (which and how many)
rubrics_metrics.description: The number and type of views required/allowed varies by jurisdiction: Hague has no maximum, EUIPO allows a maximum of seven views for RCD, USPTO expects a minimum of seven and preferably 8–10 for complex designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When both EU and US are designated, prioritize perspective views in low numbers (1–7) and place essential orthographic and explanatory views (cross-section, exploded, detail) early. Numbering of reproductions is decisive for which views EUIPO will consider among the first seven. Recommended practice: include six orthographic views plus several perspective views; at USPTO seven views is absolute minimum; more may be necessary to obtain full disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on adding 'new material' in later reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional reproductions may sometimes be added after an Office Action, but they may not introduce 'new material'—i.e., anything visible that was not evident from the original reproductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an added reproduction reveals new visible features not apparent in the original filing, the addition will be refused and the initial refusal may become final. Example: adding a bottom view of a sports shoe later is often not allowed if that view reveals new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproduction type (photos, CAD, line drawings) and presentation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDA may use photos (color or B/W), CAD drawing, line drawing or other graphics but photos must have a neutral background and no extraneous objects; reproductions must not include numbering or geometric/other information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National offices differ: USPTO generally only accepts line drawings (photos only in rare cases and color only with special petition). For US designation, prefer line drawings (or USPTO‑approved line drawings) as they are often suitable worldwide. Avoid embedded annotations or numbers in images.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface shading and shading rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When using line drawings, surface shading is advised to show contours and distinguish solid vs open elements. Common allowed types include rectilinear shading and dotted shading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surface shading is in many cases not allowed to be added after filing (would be 'new matter' and may shift application date). Jurisdictional differences: US, EU and Japan accept shading in line drawings; South Korea does not allow hatching/shading in the six mandatory orthographic views (shading only permitted in additional views). Use USPTO‑approved shading conventions when possible for broader acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual disclaimers and use of dotted lines
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim protection for only part of a product, visual disclaimers can be used—commonly dotted lines or color shading indicate excluded parts; WIPO allows dotted lines or color shading as visual disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation varies by jurisdiction: EU and Japan allow dotted lines to show context without claiming it; USPTO may treat such reference views as normal views (risking refusal). Dotted lines can be interpreted as part of the design (e.g., stitching) in EU practice. Alternatives include color shading, blurring, or boundary outlines. EUIPO does not accept verbal disclaimers; UKIPO does. Avoid ambiguous dotted lines (Apple v Samsung example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple application / Unit/Unity of Design requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: An IDA can contain up to 100 designs provided they fall in the same Locarno class, but some national offices refuse multiple applications due to Unit/Unity of Design requirements (e.g., US and Russia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If national offices refuse multiples, applicants may need to file separate national applications which must meet local drawing/reproduction requirements (and cannot introduce new matter). Note jurisdictional trends: South Korea and Japan have moved toward accepting multiple applications (Korea since 2017; Japan since 2020). Consider national refiling implications (different reproduction types, dotted line vs shading rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration of logos as designs (Locarno class 32‑00)
rubrics_metrics.description: Locarno class 32‑00 covers graphic symbols, logos, surface patterns and decoration; some jurisdictions allow registration of logos as designs but only a few accept logo registrations as designs in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design registration protects the graphic element itself and allows action against unauthorized use regardless of product—different in scope from trademark protection. Many countries are nominally in Locarno class 32‑00 but few accept logos as designs; South Korea excludes class 32‑00 designs even when applied via WIPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description of characteristic features
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries require a written description of the characteristic features of the design; failure to include one may negatively affect filing date or prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A written description, where required, can also limit the scope of protection. Check target jurisdictions' requirements on whether and how to include a descriptive statement and the possible filing date effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional differences and choice of filing route (Hague vs national)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantive design law and formal requirements vary widely among participating countries: WIPO checks formalities only, but individual IPOs apply diverging examination rules (limited absolute grounds in EU vs full novelty examination in US/Japan/South Korea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because one design application may not meet all national requirements worldwide, applicants should assess whether the international route is the best option versus national filing and should obtain local counsel advice. Consider speed (Hague can be slower than EUIPO), publication deferment availability (many countries like the US do not provide it), and overall cost-benefit (fees may not be cheaper).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical filing strategy and ordering/numbering of reproductions
rubrics_metrics.description: The order and numbering of reproductions can affect which views are considered by national offices (e.g., EUIPO considers only the first seven views).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most informative perspective views at front (low numbers 1–7) followed by essential orthographic views and explanatory cross-sections. Put less informative orthographic views (flat/undeclared bottom or back) later with higher numbers so they are disregarded where a maximum applies. Numbering is decisive for multi‑jurisdictional assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations to minimize pitfalls (procedural and policy suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ways to maximize opportunities and minimize pitfalls include IPOs providing timely and quality examinations, further harmonization of standards for examination, and awareness-raising efforts by governments and IPOs about Hague System opportunities for SMEs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a practitioner perspective this implies monitoring and engaging with harmonization initiatives, selecting representative jurisdictions carefully, and ensuring clear, high-quality reproductions and local counsel input to address divergent national practices.
